step1_summary: Chief complaint: New onset dry, red, itchy skin on arms and hands

History of present illness: Began a few days ago, noticed after a recent swimming session; progressively itchy/dry; no spots/pustules, no cracking, no discharge or bleeding; coconut butter not relieving; no fevers, sweats, vomiting, diarrhea
Aggravating/alleviating factors: Possibly triggered after swimming (chlorinated pool); stress at work; coconut butter tried without benefit
Past medical history: None significant; no prior eczema or dermatitis; possible lactose intolerance
Medications: Microgynon (combined oral contraceptive pill); no regular other meds
Allergies: None documented to drugs; possible lactose intolerance
Family history: Father – asthma; Mother – hay-fever; no known family skin disorders
Social history: 26-year-old female; primary school teacher; lives alone; recent high stress; non-smoker; minimal alcohol; no recreational drugs
Vital signs / exam: Not performed on call; patient reports red, dry, itchy rash limited to arms/hands; no systemic signs (afebrile, well-appearing)

V: Small-vessel cutaneous vasculitis: Could present with new rash, but lack of palpable purpura or systemic signs makes it less likely
I: Scabies infestation: Intensely pruritic rash on hands/arms; however, usually spreads to webs/finger, trunk and often worse at night
Superficial fungal infection (tinea corporis): Red, itchy patches possible but usually ring-shaped with central clearing—description doesn’t fit well
N: Cutaneous T-cell lymphoma (mycosis fungoides): Chronic pruritic patches/plaques—very unlikely given acute onset
D: Atopic dermatitis (eczema): Dry pruritic erythematous patches, stress-related flare, background family atopy (asthma/hay-fever)
I2: Drug eruption from Microgynon: Generalized pruritic rash possible, but she’s presumably taken OCP for some time and eruption is localized
C: Ichthyosis vulgaris: Generalized lifelong dry skin—does not match acute onset
A: Allergic contact dermatitis (e.g., to chlorine, soaps, detergents): Localized itchy erythema appearing after swimming
T: Irritant contact dermatitis (chlorinated pool water): Direct chemical irritation causing acute dry, red, pruritic areas on exposed surfaces
E: Hypothyroidism-related xerosis: Chronic dry skin & fatigue, but no other hypothyroid symptoms and acute onset

step3_ranked_ddx.diagnosis: Irritant contact dermatitis (chlorine exposure from swimming pool)
step3_ranked_ddx.explanation: Acute onset within days after swimming; lesions on exposed arms/hands; red, dry, itchy without systemic signs; coconut butter ineffective; common reaction to pool chlorine especially with winter dry skin.

step3_ranked_ddx.diagnosis: Atopic dermatitis (eczema) triggered by stress/dry weather
step3_ranked_ddx.explanation: Pruritic erythematous dry patches; personal stress and dry weather noted; strong family atopy history (asthma, hay-fever); typical in young adults though she lacks prior episodes.

step3_ranked_ddx.diagnosis: Allergic contact dermatitis (e.g., chlorine, soap, detergent)
step3_ranked_ddx.explanation: Similar presentation to irritant dermatitis but immune-mediated; temporal link to swimming; localized distribution; absence of systemic symptoms.
Pruritus prominent, may involve hands, but usually spreads, intensely itchy at night, often papules/burrows; history doesn’t mention these.
Drug eruptions can itch, but tend to be more generalized and she has been on OCP previously without issue; localization to arms & onset after swim reduce likelihood.

supporting_evidence: Rash appeared a few days ago directly after swimming
Distribution on arms/hands—areas most exposed to pool water
Dry, red, itchy without vesicles or systemic symptoms
opposing_evidence: Patient has swum before without problems

supporting_evidence: Family history of atopic disease (asthma, hay-fever)
opposing_evidence: No prior personal history of eczema
Onset clearly linked to swimming episode

supporting_evidence: Temporal relationship to swimming (possible chlorine sensitivity)
Localized to areas in direct contact with agent
opposing_evidence: No mention of vesicles/oozing often seen in allergic ACD
No nocturnal predominance, papules, burrows, or spread to trunk/groin
Living alone, no reported contacts with similar symptoms

supporting_evidence: General concept that OCPs can cause rashes
opposing_evidence: Likely longstanding medication with no previous issues
